newsitem.title: USA: Internet could solve shareholder disputes - SEC.
newsitem.headline: Internet could solve shareholder disputes - SEC.

text.p: Widespread use of the Internet could eliminate many of the communication problems shareholders face talking to corporations -- including some disputes that are taken to the Securities and Exchange Commission, an SEC commissioner said on Tuesday.

Speaking at an institutional investors conference here, SEC commissioner Steven Wallman said sweeping changes need to be made to Rule 14a-8, the federal regulation that governs shareholder resolutions.
Ultimately, use of the Internet could render that rule obsolete, he added.
"We clearly have an opportunity here, through technology, to provide a supplement -- a replacement, ultimately -- for 14a-8," he said.
Wallman proposed a system in which shareholders could talk to each other, and to corporate board members, about their concerns via some form of Web site.

Such an ongoing, informal discussion would help resolve issues early on, he said. Under the current system, shareholders are forced to cement their positions in writing to have them included in company proxies, and they only have one opportunity a year to do so.
This often leads to disputes as to which resolutions should be included in the proxies, which must then be resolved by the SEC.
"I think it is inappropriate for us to make these sorts of decisions," Wallman told his audience.

The greatest barrier to establishing a new, on-line system is validation, he said in an interview after the conference. Currently there is no widely accepted method of ensuring that suggestions come only from shareholders, or of finding out how much clout each contributor has.
However, he added that an on-line system could make the question of how much stock a shareholder owns less important.
"One of the great things that the Web provides is a leveling effect that allows the voice of the small shareholder to get in there," he said.
But until such a system is practical, an amended Rule 14a-8 is the best alternative, he said.

He proposed a series of changes that would weed out frivolous resolutions and allow some types of proposals currently excluded from corporate proxies -- for example those involving employment practices -- to be included.

Wallman encouraged members of the audience to push for these reforms. He also advocated the "decimalization" of American trading -- a change that would see U.S. stock prices quoted to the penny, rather than in fractions.
"We are the only markets in the world that trade in eighths," he said. "It costs people a tremendous amount of money."
He estimated the annual cost to individual investors of the fractional method of price quoting to be between $5 billion and $10 billion per year.
